passage:
[1] The sign on the shed said STRAND BOATS in letters that had once been red, and under it, smaller, BY APPOINTMENT, which my mother said meant that Mr. Strand did not like people. She had arranged the job anyway, through a cousin of a cousin, and on the first Monday of June she left me at the gravel turnout with a lunch bag and the advice to ask questions. I did not ask any that first week. Mr. Strand did not give me the chance. He handed me a broom.

[2] The shed was long and low and smelled of cedar and of something sharper underneath, which I later learned was the bedding compound he spread between planks. In the middle of the floor, upside down on a row of sawhorses, sat the bones of a boat: a keel, a stem curving up at one end like the neck of a heron, and a line of molds, plywood shapes that gave the hull its outline until the real ribs could take over the job. Seventeen feet, he told me, when I asked how long it would be, and that was the most he said about it until July.

[3] For three weeks I swept, sorted screws, and planed strips of cedar for the planking. Planing was the only thing he corrected. He would take the plane out of my hands without a word, sight down the strip, and give it back, and I would understand that I had been pushing too hard at the end of the stroke and rounding the edge over. I learned to stop a stroke the way you stop speaking when someone else begins. By the end of June my strips came off the bench square, and he stopped sighting them, which I took, after some thought, as the closest thing to a compliment the shed was going to offer.

[4] The ribs were oak, and they had to be bent. Mr. Strand had a steam box, a plywood coffin fed by a hose from a kettle on a propane burner, and the ribs went in for about an hour per inch of thickness, until the wood went soft as leather. Then you had perhaps a minute to get a rib out, carry it to the hull, and bend it into place against the molds before it set. He did the first six himself while I held the clamps. On the seventh he stepped back and nodded at the box.

[5] I cracked it. I felt it go before I heard it, a give in my palms that was wrong, and then a sound like a knuckle. A splinter the length of my hand lifted from the outside of the curve. I stood holding the ruined rib and waited for him to say something, and when he did not, I said it for him: I was sorry, I had been too slow, I would pay for the oak.

[6] "You weren't slow," he said. He took the rib from me and turned it so the side faced up. "Look." The lines of the grain did not run straight along the piece; halfway down they wandered off the edge, like a road leaving a map. "It was going to break there whoever bent it. I should have looked. Next time you look." He tossed it on the scrap pile and pulled another from the box, and his voice was so ordinary that I almost missed that he had just taken the blame.

[7] After that I looked. I learned to read a rib before it went into the box, to put aside the ones whose grain ran out, to bend with the growth rings rather than across them. By August I was bending every rib on the starboard side while he did the port, and we met at the stern without speaking, the two halves of the boat matching closely enough that he ran his hand along them and grunted.

[8] On my last day the hull was planked and turned right side up, and I asked him when it would go in the water. In the spring, he said; it belonged to a man in Duluth who wanted it for his grandchildren. I said I would like to see it launched. He considered that for longer than I expected. "You'll be in school," he said finally. "Don't build for the launch. The launch is the owner's. What you get is this part." He tapped the starboard rail, my side, and went back to his bench, and I stood in the doorway a while, understanding that I had been paid.
prompt: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?
choices: A narrator recalls a summer with a man of few words in which she learned a craft and a way of regarding her own work.
A narrator recalls how a cracked oak rib nearly cost her an apprenticeship that had only just begun to go well.
A narrator recalls a summer job she resented at first and then came to hope she could keep through the school year.
A narrator recalls a quiet contest with an older craftsman over which of them could finish framing a half of the hull first.
correct_answer: A narrator recalls a summer with a man of few words in which she learned a craft and a way of regarding her own work.
explanation: The narrator moves from sweeping and planing to reading grain and bending ribs on her own, and the closing scene turns on Strand's "Don't build for the launch" and her sense that she "had been paid" - a skill and an attitude toward the work. She never says she resented the job, and she does not ask to stay past the summer; Strand reminds her she will "be in school." The cracked rib is followed by Strand taking the blame, not by any threat to her place. The two halves of the hull are built side by side "without speaking" and checked for how well they match, with no race between them.

choices: measure each oak rib for length before it was put into the steam box.
lift the keel off the floor so that the stem could be planed from below.

prompt: As it is used in paragraph 4 ("against the molds before it set"), the word "set" most nearly means:
choices: was scheduled.
was put into position.
sank out of sight.
became fixed in shape.
correct_answer: became fixed in shape.
explanation: The steamed oak goes "soft as leather," and the builder has "perhaps a minute" to bend it before it "set" - that is, before it stiffens into whatever shape it then holds. "Was positioned" describes what the builder does to the rib, not the deadline the rib imposes; the sentence already says the rib is put "into place." "Was scheduled" is a sense for events, not wood. "Sank out of sight" is the sense used of the sun, and nothing in the shed disappears.

accepted responsibility for the failure without making a point of it.

Each line ran on the time of some city it had chosen, and a large station might display several clocks, each correct for a different company. By most counts the railroads were keeping more than fifty separate times, and a traveler changing trains could find that the hour itself had changed with them.

[3] What is striking is how quickly the change took hold. Within a short time most of the country's large cities had followed the railroads, and newspapers that had mocked the plan as "railroad time" were printing it as simply the time. Congress did not write the zones into law until 1918, some thirty-five years later, and that delay says a great deal: by then the government was ratifying an arrangement that business had made and the public had already accepted. In the meantime, an international conference held in Washington in 1884 chose the meridian through Greenwich, England, as the world's starting line for longitude, the same line from which the American zones were already measured. The zones show that a coordinated private effort could reorganize something as basic as the hour.

[1] A woodcut is made by taking things away. The printmaker draws on a plank, then cuts out everything that is not to print, leaving the lines and shapes standing in relief like a low plateau. Ink is rolled across the surface, paper is laid on top and rubbed or pressed, and what transfers is whatever the knife spared. Every white in the finished print is a place where wood used to be. It is a strange way to make a picture, and Agnes Holt, who has been cutting blocks in a converted dairy barn for more than thirty years, likes to say that its strangeness is the whole point. "In drawing you add until it's right," she told me. "Here you remove until it's right, and you can't put anything back."

[2] That irreversibility shapes everything about how she works. Holt makes her color prints by what printers call the reduction method. Instead of carving a separate block for each color, as the Japanese masters of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries did, she uses a single block for the entire image. She cuts away what should remain white and prints the whole edition in the palest color. Then she cuts away what should remain that pale color and prints the next color over it, on every sheet. Then she cuts again. By the time the darkest color goes down, most of the block has been carved away, and the earlier states of the image exist nowhere but on the paper. There can be no second edition. If a sheet is spoiled in the fifth color, the four colors beneath it are lost with it.

[3] Collectors sometimes take the method's limits for a marketing device, a way of guaranteeing scarcity. Holt finds the suggestion funny. She prints editions of twenty or thirty not because small numbers sell but because thirty sheets is about what she can register by hand without losing her accuracy, and because the block will not survive the cutting anyway. The scarcity is a side effect. What interests her is the commitment the method asks for: each color must be decided before the next can be imagined in wood, so the image is planned backward, from light to dark, and she cannot see it whole until it is finished.

[4] The prints themselves wear that history openly. Holt works in cherry and, lately, in a coarse local basswood, and she does not sand the grain flat. In her large print of a frozen pond, the swirl of the wood shows through the gray of the ice as a pale ripple, so that the surface seems to move under the stillness. A viewer who knows nothing of how the image was made still reads that ripple as part of the pond. A viewer who knows reads it twice: as water, and as the tree the block was cut from.

[5] This doubleness is, I think, what separates her work from the clean, flat color that printmakers have long been able to get by other means. A screenprint can lay down a gray more even than anything a plank will give. Holt does not want the even gray. She wants the mark of resistance, the place where the knife met a knot and had to turn, the faint ghost where a color printed slightly thin. Asked whether she minds those irregularities, she said the question had it backward: they are the reason she does not simply paint.

[6] It would be easy to make her into a romantic figure, the lone craftsman defending the handmade against the machine. She resists that, too. She uses a motorized press for her larger sheets, buys her paper from a mill that sells it by the thousand, and has no objection to digital tools for planning a design. Her loyalty is not to the past but to a particular kind of difficulty. "The block tells you no," she said. "Most of what I know, I learned from the no."

[1] A sockeye salmon that hatches in a gravel bed in British Columbia may spend its first year or two in a lake, ride the current down to the Pacific as a young fish about the length of a finger, and then disappear into the open ocean for a couple of years, ranging across hundreds or even thousands of kilometers of water. When it is ready to spawn, it comes back, and not merely to the right coast or the right river but, in most cases, to the very stream where it hatched. How a fish with no map manages that feat has occupied biologists for more than seventy years, and the answer they have arrived at is not one mechanism but two, each suited to a different part of the journey.

[2] The first part to be explained was the last part of the trip. In the 1950s the zoologist Arthur Hasler, working at the University of Wisconsin, proposed that young salmon memorize the smell of their home stream, a blend of minerals, plants, and soil chemistry particular to each watershed, and later follow that smell upstream. In one well-known test, researchers in Washington State caught salmon that had already returned to one of two branches of a creek, blocked the nasal openings of some of them, and released all of them below the fork. Most of the fish that could smell went back to the branch they had chosen before. The fish that could not were divided far more evenly between the two branches.

[3] Later work made the idea harder to doubt. In the 1970s, hatchery salmon raised in Wisconsin were exposed as juveniles to a synthetic chemical not found in local streams. Years later, when that chemical was dripped into a chosen stream during the spawning season, fish that had been exposed to it turned up there in large numbers. The salmon had not inherited a map of their river. They had learned a smell during a brief window early in life and kept it.

[4] Smell, though, cannot explain the ocean leg. A stream's chemical signature is diluted beyond detection long before it reaches the open sea, and a salmon a thousand kilometers offshore has nothing to follow. For decades the ocean stage remained a puzzle, and the proposed answers, among them the sun, the stars, and the ocean currents, did little to explain how precisely the fish arrive at their home coast.

[5] The most persuasive answer so far is magnetic. Earth's magnetic field varies in strength and in the angle at which its lines meet the surface, and the combination differs from place to place, so a particular stretch of coast has something like a magnetic address. The hypothesis is that a young salmon records the address of the place where it enters the sea and later swims until it finds that address again. The evidence is partly historical. Sockeye returning to British Columbia's Fraser River must pass Vancouver Island by either a northern or a southern channel, and fishery records kept over several decades showed that the share taking each route shifted as the magnetic field at the two entrances slowly drifted, much as the hypothesis predicts. Laboratory work has added support: young hatchery salmon placed in magnetic fields matching different points in the ocean have tended to orient in the direction that would carry them toward their feeding grounds.

[6] Together the two senses form a relay. Magnetism brings the fish within range of its home coast; smell takes over there and guides it, fork by fork, up the river to its stream. Neither system is perfect, and that turns out to matter. A small share of returning salmon, often a few percent, stray into streams other than the ones where they hatched. To a fisheries manager that can look like error. Over long stretches of time, though, strays are how salmon colonize rivers newly opened by retreating glaciers or by the removal of dams, and a population that never strayed would have no way to spread.
